title: Caring for the Father Who Wasn't Always There
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] My father was rarely present when I was growing up, working long stretches away from home, and missing most birthdays and school events entirely.
Narrator: When I became an adult, I told myself I owed him nothing beyond basic politeness, given how distant those early years had genuinely felt.
Narrator: [carefully] Then, two years ago, he became seriously ill, and suddenly there was no one else nearby who could reasonably take on his daily care.
Narrator: If I had refused, people would have understood, considering everything he missed, and nobody would have openly blamed me for walking away.
Narrator: [reflective] Even so, I moved him into my apartment, adjusted my work schedule around his appointments, and started learning how to manage his medications properly.
Narrator: Some mornings, resentment still surfaces unexpectedly, especially when I'm exhausted, and I catch myself wondering why I'm doing this for someone so often absent.
Narrator: [honestly] However, I remind myself that caring for him isn't really a reward I'm giving him for good fathering, since that was never how this obligation worked.
Narrator: It's something I do because of who I want to remain, regardless of who he happened to be during those earlier years of my life.
Narrator: [seriously] A friend once asked whether I had finally forgiven him, expecting a simple, satisfying answer to a genuinely complicated question.
Narrator: I told her honestly that forgiveness and duty don't always arrive together, and that I'm still working through the first while fully practicing the second.
Narrator: [gently] Some evenings, though, while helping him into bed, he'll say something small, thank you, or I'm sorry, and it briefly softens something old inside me.
Narrator: I don't expect those moments to erase an entire childhood of absence, and I've stopped hoping they eventually will.
Narrator: [encouraging] What matters more to me now is that when I stand before Allah one day, I will have done my part, whatever he did or failed to do with his.
Narrator: That thought alone gets me through the harder mornings, even the ones where forgiveness still feels frustratingly out of reach.
